la:verb:licet.gloss: to be allowed; to be permitted
senses: to be allowed; to be permitted
la:verb:licet.html:
lĭcet, cŭit and cĭtum est, 2 (old form, licessit for licuerit, ;
imp. liceto, Lex ap. ), v. n. and impers. [root lic-; Gr. λιπ-; v. 1. liceo], it is lawful, it is allowed or permitted; one may or can, one is at liberty to do so and so; constr. with neutr. of the demonstr. or rel. pron., with inf. or a subject-clause, with or without a dat., or dat. and inf., with ut or (more freq.) with the simple subj., or entirely absol.
With neutr. of the demonstr. or rel. pron. as a subject, with or without a dat.: licere id dicimus, quod legibus, quod more majorum institutisque conceditur. Neque enim quod quisque potest, id ei licet,: cui facile persuasi, mihi id, quod rogaret, ne licere quidem, non modo non lubere,: quid deceat vos, non quantum liceat vobis, spectare debetis,; cf.: si hominibus tantum licere judicas, quantum possunt: vide, ne, etc.,: si illud non licet, Saltem hoc licebit,: neque idem ubique aut licet aut decorum est, : quod in foro non expedit, illic nec liceat,: sin et poterit Naevius id quod lubet et ei lubebit, quod non licet, quid agendum est?: nihil, quod per leges liceret,: cui tantum de te licuit?; : cui tantum fata licere In generum voluere tuum,; cf.: tantumque licere horruit,.—Rarely in plur.: cum in servum omnia liceant, est, etc.,.—
With inf. or a subject-clause, with or without a dat.: neque terram inicere, neque cruenta Convestire corpora mihi licuit, Enn. ap. (Trag. v. 168 Vahl.): licet nemini contra patriam ducere exercitum,: ut tibi id facere liceat,: M. Catoni licuit Tusculi se in otio delectare,: sceleris crimine liceat Cn. Pompeio mortuo, liceat multis aliis carere,; Sulp. ap. ; : quaerere, qui licuerit aedificare navem senatori,: meamet facta mihi dicere licet,.—Without a dat.: introire in aedes numquam licitum est,: impune optare istuc licet,: modo liceat vivere,: licetne scire ex te?: hic subitam rerum commutationem videre licuit,; : si facere omnino non licebit,: licet ora ipsa cernere iratorum,; cf. : licet hoc videre,; ; ; ; : veretur ne non liceat tenere hereditatem,: licetne extra ordinem in provocantem hostem pugnare?: poscere ut perculsis instare liceat,. —With inf. pass. (cf. Krebs, Antibarb. p. 660 sq.): intellegi jam licet, nullum fore imperium,: idque e pontificio jure intellegi licet,; cf.: his cognosci licuit, quantum, etc.,; : evocari ex insula Cyprios non licet,: in senatu dici nihil liceat,: coöptari sacerdotem licebat,: in eum ordinem coöptari licet,: id primum in poëtis cerni licet,; .—The noun of the subject-clause is regularly in the acc.: licet me id scire quid sit?: non licet hominem esse, etc.,: si licet me latere,: hocine me miserum non licere meo modo ingenium frui!; cf.: eodem ut jure uti senem Liceat, id. Hec. prol. alt. 3: non licet me isto tanto bono uti,: cum non liceret Romae quemquam esse, etc.,, § 100: ex eis locis, in quibus te habere nihil licet,, § 45: quare licet etiam mortalem esse animum judicantem aeterna moliri,: cur his per te frui libertate sua, cur denique esse liberos non licet? B. and K. (al. liberis; v.infra).—So with esse: liceat esse miseros,; cf.: medios esse jam non licebit,; ; Klotz N. cr.; also with fieri: ut eum liceat ante tempus consulem fieri,: ut jam liceat una comprehensione omnia complecti non dubitantemque dicere, etc.,: haec praescripta servantem licet magnifice vivere,: licet tamen opera prodesse multis, beneficia petentem, etc.,.—So with acc. with a subject-inf., esse or fieri, even when licet is accompanied by the dat.: si civi Romano licet esse Gaditanum,: potest incidere quaestio, An huic esse procuratorem liceat?: procuratorem tibi esse non licuit, Zumpt N. cr.: mihi non licet esse piam,: is erat annus, quo per leges ei consulem fieri liceret Oud. N. cr.—But more freq., in this case, there is an attraction of the predicate-noun to the dative dependent on licet.—Hence,
Licet alicui with inf., esp. with esse: per hanc tibi cenam incenato esse hodie licet,: per hanc curam quieto tibi licet esse,: licuit esse otioso Themistocli,; cf.: ut tibi abesse liceat, et esse otioso,, A, 1: quare

judici mihi non esse liceat, : ut iis ingratis esse non liceat,: quo in genere mihi neglegenti esse non licet,: cur iis per te frui libertate sua, cur denique esse liberis non licet? (B. and K. liberos; v.supra): quibus otiosis ne in communi quidem otio liceat esse,: quibus licet jam esse fortunatissimis,: illis timidis et ignavis licet esse,.—With other verbs than esse: ut sibi per te liceat innocenti vitam in egestate degere,: cum postulasset ... ut sibi triumphanti urbem invehi liceret,— Very rarely, in this construction, the dative with licet is wanting, and is to be supplied from the connection: atqui licet esse beatis (sc. iis),: licet eminus esse Fortibus,: Hannibal precatur deos ut incolumi cedere atque abire liceat,: sibi vitam filiae suā cariorem fuisse, si liberae ac pudicae vivere licitum fuisset,. Cf. on this and the preced. construction, Krüger, Untersuchungen, vol. iii. p. 359 sq.; Ruddim. 2, p. 15; Zumpt, Gram. § 601; Madv. Gram. § 393, c. and obs. 1.—

With ut, and more freq. with the simple subj.: neque jam mihi licet neque est integrum, ut, etc.,: facto nunc laedat licet,: mea quidem causa salvos sis licet,: ludas licet,: fremant omnes licet,: sed omnia licet concurrant,: ex qua licet pauca degustes,: vel ipsi hoc dicas licet,: quamvis licet insectemur istos, metuo ne soli philosophi sint,; cf. ; : sequatur Hermagoram licebit,; : sis pecore et multa dives tellure licebit,: detrahat auctori multum fortuna licebit,; . Cf. also under II. a.—(ε) As a v. impers. absol., with or without dat.: immo, aliis si licet, tibi non licet,: cum licitum est ei,: nec crederem mihi impunius Licere,: quod profecto faciam, si mihi per ejusdem amicitiam licebit,: Ph. Sed quaeso, hominem ut jubeas arcessi. He. Licet, that may be or may be done, I have no objection, : si per vos licet,: id quod postea, si per vos, judices, licitum erit, aperietur,: dum per aetatem licet,: fruare, dum licet,; cf.: dum licet, loquimini mecum,: sic ut quimus, aiunt, quando, ut volumus, non licet,: ut id, quoad posset, quod fas esset, quoad liceret, populi ad partes daret,.
Transf. When licet introduces a subordinate proposition, which makes a concession, without abandoning the main proposition, it is used as a conjunction corresponding to quamvis, quamquam, etsi. In late Latin it is, like these, connected with the indicative, and in the class. per. it is not unfreq. opposed to tamen and certe in the main proposition; even if, although, notwithstanding.
With subj. (class.): quoniam quidem semel suscepi, licet hercules undique omnes mihi minae et terrores periculaque impendeant omnia, succurram atque subibo,: improbitas, licet adversario molesta sit, judici invisa est,: in comoedia maxime claudamus: licet Varro Musas Plautino dicat sermone locuturas fuisse, si Latine loqui vellent; licet, etc.,: vita brevis est, licet supra mille annos exeat,: licet ingens janitor ... exsanguis terreat umbras,. —With part. for subj.: isque, licet caeli regione remotos, mente deos adiit,.—With a corresp. tamen: licet laudem Fortunam, tamen, ut ne Salutem culpem,: licet saepius tibi hujus generis litteras mittam ... sed tamen, etc.,: licet tibi significarim, ut ad me venires, tamen, etc.,; ; : licet ergo non sint confirmati testamento, a me tamen, ut confirmati, observabuntur,; : constet illi licet fides et benevolentia, tranquillitas tamen, etc., Sen. Tranq. Anim. 7, 6.—With ellips. of subj.: immatura licet, tamen huc non noxia veni (sc. venias),.—With a corresp. certe: licet enim haec quivis arbitratu suo reprehendat ... certe levior reprehensio est,.—
With indic. (post-class.): licet inter gesta et facta videtur quaedam esse subtilis differentia, attamen, etc.,; : licet directae libertates deficiunt, attamen, etc.,: obduxi licet arma, sum Priapus, Poëta ap. Anth. Lat. 5, 218; ; .—
As an adv. with adj. or part., although (post-class.): licet contumacissimum, tamen efficacissimum, etc.,: miles, licet membris vigentibus firmus, se solum circumspicit,; ; .—Hence,
lĭcens, entis, P. a., free, unrestrained, uncurbed, bold, forward, presumptuous, licentious.
Of persons (only poet. and in post-class. prose): quam audaces et quam licentes sumus qui, etc.,: unde licens Fabius sacra Lupercus habet,: turba licens, Naides improbae,.—
Of inanim. and abstr. things (once in Cic.; elsewh. only poet. and in post-Aug. prose): licentior dithyrambus,: hic tibi multa licet sermone licentia tecto Dicere,: joci,: licentior epistula, Plin. N. H. prooem. § 1: imperium,: vita,. —Hence, adv.: lĭcenter, freely, according to one's own pleasure or fancy; and, in a bad sense, without restraint, boldly, impudently, licentiously (class.): at quam licenter!: ut ingredi libere, non ut licenter videatur errare,: Graeci licenter multa,: aliquid facere,.—Comp.: (servos) licentius, liberius, familiarius cum domina vivere,: Romanos, remoto metu, laxius licentiusque futuros,more remiss in their discipline,: gerere res communes,: ausi aliquid,: si quid licentius dixerint,: translata,; : Liberum et Cererem pro vino et pane licentius, quam ut fori severitas ferat,; .—
lĭcĭtus, a, um, P. a., permitted, allowed, allowable, lawful (poet. and post-Aug. for permissus, honestus): sermo,: torus,: acies,: negotiatio,: contractus,.—In plur. as subst.: lĭcĭta, ōrum, n., things that are lawful: ipse per licita atque illicita foedatus,.—Hence, adv., in two forms: lĭcĭtē and lĭcĭtō, rightfully, lawfully (post-class. for juste, honeste, legitime).—Form licite, .— Form licito,; Cod. Th. 11, 8, 3.

senses: to have a price; to fetch; to value
la:verb:liceo.html:
lĭcĕo, cŭi, cĭtum, 2, v. n.
Sanscr. root rik-, riktas, empty; Gr. λιπ-, λείπω, leave; Lat. lic-, linquo, licet, liceor; cf. Germ. leihen, verleihen
,
to be for sale; to have a price put upon it, to be valued, esteemed at so much.
Lit. (rare but class.): omnia vaenibunt, quiqui licebunt, praesenti pecunia,: quanti licuisse tu scribis (hortos),how much they were valued at,: unius assis Non umquam pretio pluris licuisse,. —
Transf., of the seller, to offer for sale, to fix the price, to value at so much (only post-Aug.): percontanti quanti liceret opera effecta, parvum nescio quid dixerat,how much he asked for them, what he held them at,: parvo cum pretio diu liceret,.

la:noun:lictor.html:
lictor (pronounced līctor, ), ōris, m.
1. ligo; cf. sqq.
,
a lictor, i. e. an attendant granted to a magistrate, as a sign of official dignity. The Romans adopted this custom from the Etrurians: Romulus cum cetero habitu se augustiorem tum maxime lictoribus duodecim sumptis (a finitima Etruria) fecit,. The lictors bore a bundle of rods, from which an axe projected. Their duty was to walk before the magistrate in a line, one after the other; to call out to the people to make way (submovere turbam); and to remind them of paying their respects to him (animadvertere, v. h. v.). The foremost one was called primus lictor: apud quem primus quievit lictor,; the last and nearest to the consul, proximus lictor, The lictors had also to execute sentences of judgment, to bind criminals to a stake, to scourge them, and to behead them, ; ; ; 26, 16.—It was necessary that lictors should be freeborn: not till the time of Tacitus were freedmen also appointed to the office. They were united into a company, and formed the decuriae apparitorum (public servants). In Rome they wore the toga, in the field the sagum, in triumphal processions a purple mantle and fasces wreathed with laurel: togulae lictoribus ad portam praesto fuerunt, quibus illi acceptis, sagula rejecerunt et catervam imperatori suo novam praebuerunt,. Only those magistrates who had potestatem cum imperio had lictors. In the earliest times the king had twelve; immediately after the expulsion of the kings, each of the two consuls had twelve; but it was soon decreed that the consuls should be preceded for a month alternately by twelve lictors,; a regulation which appears to have been afterwards, although not always, observed,; Cæsar was the first who restored the old custom,.—The decemvirs had, in their first year of office, twelve lictors each one day alternately, ; in their second year each had twelve lictors to himself,.— The military tribunes with consular power had also twelve lictors,; and likewise the interrex,.—The dictator had twenty-four, Dio, 54, 1; Polyb. 3, 87; Plut. Fab. 4; the magister equitum only six, Dio, 42, 27. The praetor urbanus had, in the earlier times, two lictors,: at enim unum a praetura tua, Epidice, abest. Ep. Quidnam? Th. Scies. Lictores duo, duo viminei fasces virgarum, ; in the provinces he had six; but in the later times the praetor had in the city, as well as in the province, six lictors, Polyb. 3, 40: cum praetor lictorem impellat et ire praecipitem jubeat,. The quaestor had lictors only in the province, when he, in consequence of the praetor's absence or death, performed the functions of propraetor, ; . Moreover, the flamen dialis, the vestals, and the magistri vicorum had lictors; these, however, appear to have had no fasces, which was also the case with the thirty lictores curiati (who summoned the curiae to vote),; ; ; .—
Transf.: lictorem feminae in publico unionem esse,a lady's mark of distinction,.

la:verb:liceor.html:
lĭcĕor, lĭcĭtus, 2,
v. dep. n. and a. [root lic-; v. 1. liceo], to bid on goods at an auction (class.).
Absol.: licetur Aebutius,: liciti sunt usque adeo, quoad, etc.,: digito liceri (because, in bidding, the finger was raised),, § 27: omnia Aeduorum vectigalia parvo pretio redemta habere, propterea, quod illo licente, contra liceri audeat nemo,to bid against,: immoderatius liceri,: nec licendi finem factum,.—
Act., to bid for, make an offer for.—With acc.: heredes Scapulae si istos hortos liceri cogitant,to bid on the gardens,; so, hortos liceri,: et centum Graecos curto centusse licetur,. —*
Trop., to appraise, estimate, value: tunc avidi matronam oculi licentur,appraise her, reckon at what price she can be robbed of her honor,.

senses: a liberty which one assumes; boldness; presumption
la:noun:licentia.html:
lĭcentĭa, ae, f.
licet
,
freedom, liberty, leave to do as one pleases, license.
In gen.: Dae. Licet ... licet ... licet. Tr. Hercules istum infelicet cum sua licentia, : nobis nostra Academia magnam licentiam dat, ut, etc.,: pueris non omnem ludendi licentiam damus,: tantum licentiae dabat gloria,: absolvendi,: lasciviendi permittere militibus,.—
In partic.
Liberty which one assumes, boldness, presumption, license: homo ad scribendi licentiam liber,: a Democrito omnino haec licentia,: per intercalandi licentiam,by arbitrary intercalation,.—Freq. of style: poëtarum,: juvenilis quaedam dicendi impunitas et licentia,: figurarum,.—
In rhet. as a figure of speech, = παρρησία, boldness, freedom of speech, : poëtica,; : declamatoria,.—
Unrestrained liberty, unbounded license, dissoluteness, licentiousness: deteriores omnes sumus licentia,: nimia illaec licentia evadet in aliquod magnum malum,: omnium rerum infinita atque intoleranda licentia,: licentia libidoque,: cupiditatum,; : habere impunitatem et licentiam sempiternam,: quorum licentiae nisi Carneades restitisset,: malle licentiam suam quam aliorum libertatem, : Sullani temporis,lawlessness,: militum,: indomitam Refrenare (licentiam),: licentiam coërcere,: in libertatibus quoque dandis nimiam licentiam compescuit lex Fufia Caninia,.—Of inanimate things: magna gladiorum est licentia, the license of the sword is great, i. e. daring murders are prevalent, : immensa licentia ponti,.—
Personified as a goddess: templum Licentiae (for Libertatis),; cf. Libertas.

la:adj:licentiosus.html:
lĭcentĭōsus, a, um, adj.
licentia
,
full of freedom or license, over-free, unbridled, unrestrained, wanton, licentious (post-Aug.): (ebor dicere) non minus est licentiosum, quam si sulfuri et gutturi subicerent in genitivo litteram o mediam, * : temeritas,.— Comp.: conversatio cum viris licentiosior,.—Sup.: libidini licentiosissimum spatium praebere,.—Adv.: lĭcentĭōsē (late Lat. and rare), .

la:adj:Licinius.html:
Lĭcĭnĭus, a,
name of a Roman gens.
The tribune C. Licinius Crassus, ; .—
The triumvir M. Licinius Crassus, ; .—
L. Licinius Crassus, the famous orator, ; .—In fem.: Lĭcĭnĭa, ae, a daughter of the orator L. Licinius Crassus, .—Also, a vestal, .—
Hence,
Lĭcĭnĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to a Licinius, Licinian: lex, of various kinds, esp. the lex de sodaliciis,; cf. the Index legum, Orell. Cic. Opera, vol. viii. p. 199 sq.: lex Licinia et Mucia de civibus redigundis,, vol. xi. p. 11 B. and K.: lex de modo agrorum,; cf. : atria, named after L. Licinius Crassus,auction-halls,; .—
Lĭcĭnĭānus, a, um, adj., Licinian: olea,introduced by a Licinius,: jugera,the lands distributed to the plebeians by C. Licinius Stolo,; .—
Lĭcĭ-nĭāni, ōrum, m., a surname of the sons and descendants of Cato the Censor, by his first wife, Licinia; to distinguish them from those by the second, who where called Salonii or Saloniani,.

la:noun:licitatio.html:
lĭcĭtātĭo, ōnis, f.
licitor
,
an offering of a price, a bidding for any thing, at sales and auctions: exquisitis palam pretiis et licitationibus factis,; : praedam ad licitationem dividere,to the highest bidders,: licitatione maxima comparare aliquid,: ad licitationem rem deducere,: licitatione vincere,to bid highest,: penes quem licitatio remansit,to whom it was knocked down,: cum contentio fructus licitationis est,.
